newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ dollar ends sharply stronger after RBNZ comment.
newsitem.headline: NZ dollar ends sharply stronger after RBNZ comment.

text.p: The New Zealand dollar closed sharply stronger on Tuesday after a Reserve Bank easing that was not seen by the market as an easing.
Dealers said the trading was wild and whippy.
The kiwi rose more than one U.S. cent after the RB's statement before closing at US$0.7067/74, down from its 0.7096 high and against 0.6985/92 at the opening.
The Trade-Weighted Index closed at 67.39 against the 66.79 opening.
Dealers said the Reserve Bank had confirmed in its six monthly Monetary Policy Statement that the New Zealand dollar was essentially a one-way bet.

The Reserve Bank assumed in its six monthly Monetary Policy Statement that the TWI should be at 66.5, rather than some market expectations of 65.0 and that would serve to underpin the currency, dealers said.
"They are basically telling the market they don't want the currency lower despite what (Reserve Bank Governor Don) Brash is telling people," said a Wellington bank chief dealer.

Dealers interpreted Treasurer Winston Peters' comments as ineffectual. Peters said he welcomed the Reserve Bank's easing of monetary policy but added he would not be interfering in the day-to-day running of the bank.
"Brash said he won't let interest rates fall so it's just a one-way bet," the chief dealer said. "We will see the currency higher."
"The bottom line is that New Zealand controls inflation by pushing the dollar whenever it rears its ugly head. Brash has to keep pushing the TWI up to get the right inflation numbers.

"It's given the green light to people wanting to buy the kiwi. He says he won't intervene in the currency and he won't let interest rates fall, so there is no reason for the kiwi to have any sustained selloff," the chief dealer said.
Another dealer said that U.S. fund managers were heavy buyers of the currency and they expect the pattern to continue.
"They had the chance to take the currency lower but decided not to take it," a dealer said.
